desc:
A chemical formula is a string made of these parts:

  • An element: one uppercase letter followed by zero or more lowercase letters, for example H, Mg, Uuo. An element may be followed by a count, a number written in digits without leading zeros (at least 1). With no count the element appears once.
  • A group: (, a non-empty formula, ), and optionally a count that multiplies every atom inside the group. No count means a multiplier of 1.

Groups may be nested. Return the total number of atoms of every element in this canonical form: element names in increasing alphabetical (ASCII) order, each followed by its total count when that count is more than 1, all joined into one string.

Examples: 'H2O' → 'H2O'; 'Mg(OH)2' → 'H2MgO2'; 'K4(ON(SO3)2)2' → 'K4N2O14S4'.
constraints: The formula is well formed as described, with letters, digits and round brackets only
Every count and multiplier is between 1 and 1,000,000 and has no leading zeros
The total count of each element is at most 10<sup>9</sup>
hints: Without brackets this is a simple scan: read a name, read a number, add to a map. What changes when brackets appear?
Counts inside brackets are only final after you see the multiplier after the ). Think about keeping a separate map for each open bracket.
Use a stack of maps. On ( push a fresh map. On ) read the optional number, pop the top map, multiply its values, and add them into the map below. Finally sort the names of the bottom map.
editorial: Parse left to right with an index. A stack of dictionaries holds the counts of every open group; the bottom dictionary is the whole formula. When you see an uppercase letter, read the following lowercase letters as the element name and the following digits as its count (default 1), and add the count to the top dictionary.

On ( push an empty dictionary. On ) read the digits after it as the multiplier (default 1), pop the top dictionary, and add each of its counts times the multiplier into the dictionary that is now on top. At the end the bottom dictionary has the totals. Sort the names, and write name alone for count 1 or name + count otherwise. The scan is linear in the length; the sort adds O(k log k) for k distinct elements, and extra space is bounded by the nesting depth times the number of distinct elements.
